extraction.name: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
extraction.description: A benchmark of 11.5K meticulously collected college-level multimodal questions from exams, quizzes, textbooks, online sources, and lecture materials, covering six disciplines, 30 subjects, 183 subfields, and 30 image types, designed to evaluate multimodal models on expert-level perception, knowledge, and reasoning.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.citeAs: Yue, X., Ni, Y., Zhang, K., Zheng, T., Liu, R., Zhang, G., Stevens, S., Jiang, D., Ren, W., Sun, Y., Wei, C., Yu, B., Yuan, R., Sun, R., Yin, M., Zheng, B., Yang, Z., Liu, Y., Huang, W., Sun, H., Su, Y., & Chen, W. (2024). MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark collection takes three stages. First, the authors went through common university majors to decide which subjects to include, selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on whether visual inputs are commonly adopted and ruling out subjects like law and linguistics. Second, they recruited over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources and to create new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations and to avoid questions with immediately available answers to reduce data contamination concerns. This process resulted in a diverse collection of 13K questions from various sources. The final benchmark contains 11.5K carefully selected questions after quality control and filtering.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions were collected from free online resources, quizzes, textbooks, other study materials, online sources, and lecture materials; the paper also states the benchmark draws from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Potential duplicate problems were identified using lexical overlap and source URL similarity, then reviewed by the authors to eliminate duplications. Problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format. Authors categorized problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems classified as very easy and not aligning with the design criteria were excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All questions were required to contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, be unambiguous, and be answerable with one of the given options or a short answer. Annotators categorized each question as multiple-choice or open-ended and annotated fields including question text, answer options, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation if available. The structured JSON format included fields for number, question type, question text, answer options, correct answer, question difficulty, and explanation. Images were inserted as file paths in the question, options, or explanations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors served as annotators to collect multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources and create new questions where necessary. The annotation protocol required accurate and consistent annotations with academic rigor. Questions had to contain one or more images, be in English, be college-level, and be unambiguous. Annotators labeled question type, question text, answer options for multiple-choice questions, the correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation if it existed. Authors also categorized problems into four difficulty levels. For error analysis, 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V error instances were analyzed by expert annotators who identified root causes based on their knowledge and golden explanations if available.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A user-friendly web interface for data annotation and verification
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A secondary review team rigorously vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence, and regular audits of random samples were conducted to ensure quality and consistency. Ambiguities or unclear data instances were flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings to establish a standardized approach for annotation. In the error analysis, expert annotators analyzed 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V error instances and identified root causes; the distribution included perceptual error (35%), lack of knowledge (29%), reasoning error (26%), textual understanding error, rejection to answer, annotation error, and answer extraction error.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors and from various disciplines and subjects; for human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent a wide range of experts in the 30 subjects, with 3 student experts per subject.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The appendix includes a Version Change Log with updates from V1 to V4: changes from V2 (Dec.18) from V1 (Nov.27), changes from V3 (Dec.21) from V2 (Dec.18), and changes from V4 (June.13) from V3 (Dec.21). Xiang Yue took the lead in the dataset release.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The annotation protocol states that annotators should avoid collecting questions that contain any private information. The benchmark covers subjects including Health & Medicine and Public Health, and example questions may include age and gender references in question content, but no dataset-level collection of personal sensitive information is explicitly described.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that monitoring progress toward Expert AGI is of intellectual and societal importance because Expert AGI could reach the substitution threshold for human labor in many industries, leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The authors believe MMMU will be instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitoring progress toward Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper states that MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations and that the manual curation process may carry biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper cautions that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and the 90th percentile of skilled adults, nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. It also states that the manual curation process may carry biases and that the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed as a benchmark to evaluate multimodal models on college-level multi-discipline multimodal understanding and reasoning, measuring perception, knowledge, and reasoning. It is divided into a few-shot development set, a validation set useful for hyperparameter selection, and a test set. The authors evaluate models in zero-shot settings and also report some few-shot results in the appendix.
